headline: School Budget Clears State Hurdle as Town Looks Inward
dek: *A landmark approval for Shaker Lane, a charter review in full swing, and a summer of civic housekeeping set the tone for a town building toward its future.*
lede: The biggest news hanging over Littleton this week arrived with quiet authority: the Massachusetts School Building Authority has approved the budget for the Shaker Lane School construction project, clearing a critical state hurdle for a community that has spent years grappling with a 64-year-old elementary building well past its prime. That approval transforms the project from aspiration into something closer to inevitability. The Shaker Lane School Building Committee has been meeting regularly since spring, and a community forum in May gave residents a chance to shape how Littleton's identity gets woven into the new design. Now, with the MSBA's blessing on the budget, the hard work of actually building shifts into a higher gear.

sections.body:
The path to a new Shaker Lane School has been methodical and, at times, painstaking. The Building Committee convened multiple times through the spring — in April, May, and again in June — working through the details that any project of this scale demands. A community forum in May invited residents to imagine what the building could say about Littleton, not just what it would house. That kind of public engagement matters, and the committee clearly understood it.

With the MSBA budget approval now in hand, the conversation shifts from whether to build to how and when. The School Committee also held a special meeting on June 25th, suggesting the school side of the equation remains active and engaged. Residents who want to follow along should expect the Building Committee to remain a fixture on the civic calendar well into the fall.

While the school project commands the loudest headlines, there is quieter but equally consequential work happening at Town Hall. The Charter Committee has met repeatedly since April — six times through June — a pace that signals genuine deliberation rather than routine check-ins. Town charters are foundational documents, the kind of thing that shapes how every other civic decision gets made, and a committee meeting that often is working through something substantial.

The Select Board and Finance Committee held a joint session in early June as well, a pairing that typically signals budget or structural questions that cross the usual committee boundaries. Together, these threads suggest Littleton is in a period of self-examination about how it governs itself — a healthy, if demanding, undertaking.

Conservation and planning boards have kept a brisk pace alongside the headline items. The Conservation Commission met multiple times through the spring and into late June, and the Clean Lakes Committee gathered again on June 25th — a reminder that Littleton's ponds and watersheds require ongoing stewardship, not just seasonal attention. The Planning Board, meanwhile, held a retreat in early June before its regular June 25th session, suggesting the board is thinking strategically about what comes next for the town's physical landscape.

One tangible expression of that strategic thinking: the Planning Board is actively soliciting resident input on transportation improvements in the Acton-Littleton area through an ongoing survey. If you live along one of those corridors and have opinions about traffic, crossings, or connections, now is the moment to make yourself heard before those plans harden.

The Finance Committee is scheduled to meet on July 9th, the first major civic gathering after this week's flurry of activity. That meeting will be worth watching for any signals about how the town's financial picture is settling after a spring of overlapping priorities — a school construction budget, a charter review, and active land-use deliberations all drawing on municipal bandwidth at once. Summer in Littleton rarely means a slowdown; it tends to mean the work continues with slightly fewer people in the room.

pull_quote: A 64-year-old building is finally getting its replacement — and the state just made it real.
threads: Finance Committee meets July 9th — watch for post-spring budget signals
Charter Committee's sustained pace suggests a proposal or draft may be taking shape; follow what emerges from Town Hall this summer

headline: School Budget Approved, Drought Bites, and King Street Stirs
dek: *A milestone for Shaker Lane, a dry summer warning, and a stretch of King Street poised for its next chapter define a busy week at the midpoint of 2026.*
lede: The biggest news to land on Littleton this week came from Boston: the Massachusetts School Building Authority formally approved the budget for the Shaker Lane School construction project, clearing a critical state-level hurdle for replacing a building that is now 64 years old. It is the kind of approval that turns years of planning meetings, community forums, and spreadsheet arguments into something real — a project with a sanctioned price tag and a path forward. The Shaker Lane Building Committee has been meeting regularly, and the School Committee convened a special session on June 25th, a sign that the work of moving from approval to action is already underway. For a town that has been weighing what to do about its aging elementary school for some time, this week marked a turning point.

sections.body: The MSBA's budget approval does not mean shovels in the ground tomorrow, but it means the project is real in the eyes of the state — and that matters enormously for financing and momentum. Community forums held earlier this spring gave residents a chance to weigh in on design direction, and the Building Committee has been keeping the public process moving with regular meetings and posted recordings. The next questions will involve timelines, site logistics, and what the town's share of costs will ultimately look like. Watch for the Building Committee and School Committee to set a more detailed public schedule in the weeks ahead.

While the school story dominated the civic conversation, a quieter but significant thread ran through the land-use calendar: King Street is getting a lot of attention from town boards. The Planning Board has a public hearing scheduled for July 9th on a stormwater management permit and site plan for a retail development at 550 King Street — labeled Phase II, with both a north and south component — and the Conservation Commission has its own public hearing on that same address penciled in for July 21st. Separately, 300 King Street, the site of Castle in the Trees Park, will also come before the Conservation Commission that same evening. That is a notable clustering of scrutiny along a single corridor, and residents who care about how that stretch of town develops will want to pay attention to both boards this month.

Also on the Planning Board's July 9th agenda is a public hearing for an affordable senior housing proposal at 410 Great Road — a project that, if it advances, would speak directly to a pressing regional need. The Zoning Board of Appeals joins the action in mid-July with hearings on properties at 27 Lake Warren Drive and 359 King Street.

Away from the meeting rooms, residents are being asked to change their daily habits in response to something harder to vote on: the weather. Littleton is currently under a Level 3 Critical Drought, the state's most serious drought designation before emergency status, and all nonessential outdoor water use is now prohibited. That means no lawn irrigation, no washing cars in the driveway, no hosing down patios — the kind of summer rituals that feel minor individually but add up across thousands of households. The Light & Water Commissioners met on June 24th, and the Conservation Commission and Clean Lakes Committee have both been active; water conditions will almost certainly remain a central concern for all of them as summer deepens.

Even in a dry summer, there is reason to get outside. The Art Lazarus Trail at Long Lake Park Conservation Area has officially opened, honoring a volunteer who gave 33 years of his life to conservation work in Littleton. A ribbon-cutting ceremony marked the occasion, and the trail now stands as both a recreational asset and a tribute to the kind of quiet, sustained civic commitment that rarely makes headlines but shapes a community profoundly. The Conservation Commission, which meets again on July 7th, also has public hearings coming up on Webster Woods Conservation Land — another reminder of how actively Littleton manages and expands the open spaces that define its character.

The Select Board held both a regular meeting and a full retreat on June 30th — a sign that the board is doing longer-horizon thinking as the second half of the year begins. Residents who attended Annual Town Meeting in the spring are invited to complete a feedback survey, a useful way for the town to improve how it runs its signature participatory democracy event. Early voting is also available for the upcoming state primary, and with the July 4th holiday landing mid-week, the Finance Committee meeting on July 9th will be one of the first chances for boards to reconvene at full speed after the holiday.

pull_quote: A 64-year-old school, a Level 3 drought, and a corridor called King Street: Littleton's summer is anything but quiet.
threads: Watch the Planning Board's July 9th hearings on 550 King Street retail Phase II and the 410 Great Road affordable senior housing proposal — two decisions that could reshape different corners of town.

The Conservation Commission's triple-header on July 21st — covering Webster Woods, Castle in the Trees Park, and 550 King Street — will test how the town balances development pressure against its conservation commitments.
With the MSBA budget approved, the Shaker Lane Building Committee's next steps on timeline, community process, and local cost-sharing will be the ones to track for school-age families.

headline: Sewers Flow, Schools Rise, and King Street Faces Its Future
dek: *A week of ribbon cuttings and public hearings signals a town actively reshaping itself from the ground up.*
lede: Littleton marked a quiet but meaningful milestone this week when the new Littleton Common Sewer System was declared fully operational after nearly two years of construction — a ribbon cutting that closes one chapter and opens another for the town center. At the same time, the Planning Board convened Thursday evening to hold public hearings on two projects that could define the next decade of growth along King Street and Great Road: a second retail phase at 550 King Street and an affordable senior housing proposal at 410 Great Road. Taken together, the sewer completion and the development hearings tell the same story — Littleton is building, deliberately, and the decisions being made in meeting rooms this summer will be felt for a generation.

sections.body:
The ribbon cutting on the Littleton Common Sewer System is the kind of civic accomplishment that rarely gets its due. Sewer projects are unglamorous by nature — they happen underground, they take years, and they only make the news when something goes wrong. This one went right. After nearly two years of construction, the system is fully operational, and it brings a basic piece of modern infrastructure to a part of town that has long needed it. It's the sort of foundational investment that makes everything else — housing, commercial development, a healthy town center — more possible.

Also on the utility front, the Littleton Electric Light and Water Department continues to make news in two very different registers. On one hand, LELWD was awarded a state grant of $285,000 to upgrade distribution equipment and reduce the impact of power outages — a meaningful win for grid reliability. On the other, the Littleton Water Department has filed a federal lawsuit to recover costs incurred removing PFAS contamination from the water supply, a fight that speaks to a problem the town did not create but is now shouldering the expense of fixing.

The Planning Board's Thursday night session was dense with consequence. The board opened public hearings on stormwater and site plans for both the second retail phase at 550 King Street and an affordable senior housing development at 410 Great Road — two projects that together represent the range of pressures on Littleton's commercial and residential corridors. The 550 King Street project will also face the Conservation Commission later this month, on July 21st, adding another layer of review before anything can move forward.

Also coming up on the 21st: a Conservation Commission hearing on Webster Woods Conservation Land and another on Castle in the Trees Park at 300 King Street. The concentration of open-space and development hearings on a single evening reflects how much is in motion along the King Street corridor right now. Residents who care about how that stretch of town looks and functions a decade from now have good reason to tune in.

The campaign to replace Shaker Lane Elementary — a 64-year-old building the town has been studying seriously for over a year — continued to gather momentum this week. The Shaker Lane School Building Committee has been meeting regularly, and a community forum earlier this spring invited residents to share ideas about how a new building might reflect Littleton's identity. The project is moving through the deliberate, multi-step process that Massachusetts school construction requires, and while no ground has been broken, the direction is clear.

Meanwhile, Littleton's schools earned recognition that gives the broader conversation some welcome context: Littleton Middle School received a Blue Ribbon nomination, and the high school earned state recognition. These are not small honors, and they serve as a reminder that the push to replace aging facilities is not a story of failure — it's a story of a community that takes its schools seriously enough to invest in them.

Beneath the meeting agendas and ribbon cuttings, a quieter emergency is unfolding. Littleton is currently under a Level 3 Critical Drought designation from MassDEP, and outdoor watering restrictions are in effect. The Water Department has reminded residents that conservation is not optional right now — it is required. The Clean Lakes Committee met in late June, and with the Conservation Commission active on multiple fronts, water — its quality, its quantity, and its governance — is very much on the town's mind this summer.

The Select Board is set to meet Monday evening, July 13th, and one of the items on the agenda reflects a growing priority: a joint meeting with the Housing Authority. Affordable housing has been threading through nearly every corner of civic life in Littleton this week — from the Planning Board hearing on the Great Road senior housing proposal, to the Affordable Housing Trust meeting scheduled for July 14th, to the Zoning Board of Appeals hearings coming up on July 16th for properties on King Street and Lake Warren Drive. The Community Preservation Committee meets July 15th, adding yet another body to the week's housing conversation. What was once a discrete policy area now feels like the connective tissue running through almost everything the town is deciding.

pull_quote: The decisions being made in meeting rooms this summer will be felt for a generation.
threads: Conservation Commission takes up Webster Woods, Castle in the Trees Park, and 550 King Street in a single session on July 21st — a hearing worth watching for anyone tracking open space and development on the King Street corridor.
The Housing Authority's joint meeting with the Select Board on July 13th could signal how the town plans to align its affordable housing tools heading into the fall.

The Shaker Lane School Building Committee's next steps will indicate whether the project is ready to advance toward a formal MSBA submission — the process that unlocks state funding for school construction.

headline: A School Week of Triumphs, Trauma, and a 64-Year Reckoning
dek: *Littleton's schools dominated the week's conversation — for reasons both proud and painful — while a new trail and a housing flurry quietly shaped the town's longer story.*
lede: It was a week that forced Littleton to hold two very different things about its schools at once. On one hand, the Massachusetts School Building Authority approved the budget for a long-anticipated replacement of the 64-year-old Shaker Lane Elementary School, a milestone that sets the town on a concrete path toward a modern building for its youngest learners. On the other hand, a former school bus aide pleaded guilty to assaulting nonverbal autistic children on a Littleton school bus in 2024, and a Marlborough man who drove a school bus in town was charged with raping a child — cases that surfaced in regional news this week and cast a shadow over the district's otherwise celebratory moment. The contrast was jarring, and it deserves to be named plainly.

sections.body:
The approval of the Shaker Lane Elementary School building budget by the MSBA is the kind of news that takes years to arrive and then lands quietly — a line item that represents thousands of hours of planning and a genuine commitment to do right by the town's children. Replacing a 64-year-old building is not a luxury; it is an acknowledgment that the structure has simply aged out of what modern education requires. The School Committee's Negotiating Subcommittee also met this week, a reminder that the human infrastructure of the district — its staff contracts — requires the same sustained attention as its physical one.

At the same time, the district's recognition streak continued. Littleton Middle School earned a nomination for a National Blue Ribbon award, the high school received state-level recognition, and five students were honored for excellence in world languages. These are genuine achievements, and they belong to the students and educators who earned them. But they sit this week alongside the guilty plea and the new charges involving school transportation — a reminder that excellence in the classroom and failures in oversight can exist in the same system, and that one does not cancel out the other.

If the schools dominated the headlines, housing quietly dominated the calendar. In a single week, the Affordable Housing Trust met, the Community Preservation Committee convened, the Housing Authority held a joint session with the Select Board, and the Planning Board gathered — all touching, in one way or another, on how Littleton grows and who gets to live here. The 01460: On the Go program also aired a segment that touched on development themes. That is a remarkable concentration of civic energy on a single subject, and it reflects both the pressure the region is under and the seriousness with which Littleton is trying to respond. The details of what each body discussed are not yet fully public, but the sheer volume of meetings signals that decisions are moving.

On a quieter note, the town officially opened the Art Lazarus Trail at Long Lake Park Conservation Area this week, honoring a volunteer whose 33 years of conservation work left a measurable mark on Littleton's open spaces. A ribbon-cutting is a small ceremony, but naming a trail for someone who gave three decades of unpaid labor is how a community says it noticed. The Littleton Conservation Trust, which organized the opening, also continues its trails hiking challenge, and a recent LCTV episode featured Conservation Trust President Dustin Neild talking about volunteering and stewardship. The Conservation Commission, meanwhile, has a virtual meeting scheduled for July 21 and a public hearing set for August 4 — the work of protecting what Lazarus helped build continues.

The Town Clerk's office is reminding residents that the state primary is scheduled for September 1, 2026, with in-person early voting already available. If that date feels distant, it isn't — summer moves fast, and the Clerk's reminder is well-timed. Separately, a state report on retiree benefit obligations showed Littleton has made consistent progress in setting aside funds for long-term costs, a detail that rarely makes front pages but matters quietly to the town's fiscal health. The Select Board meets again on July 27.

pull_quote: Excellence in the classroom and failures in oversight can exist in the same system — and one does not cancel out the other.
threads: Watch for updates on the Shaker Lane Elementary School project timeline and what the MSBA budget approval means for the next phases of design and construction.
The Conservation Commission's July 21 meeting and August 4 public hearing may offer early signals about what development pressures are reaching Littleton's wetlands and open spaces.
With the state primary on September 1 and early voting underway, residents should confirm their registration and polling information with the Town Clerk's office now.

headline: A New School Takes Shape While Trails and Honors Bloom
dek: *Littleton's biggest week in recent memory blends a long-awaited school rebuild, fresh conservation paths, and a string of academic honors—with a sobering court verdict in the background.*
lede: The defining story of this week in Littleton is one that has been building for years: the town is moving in earnest to replace Shaker Lane School, a 64-year-old elementary building that has outlived its usefulness. The Massachusetts School Building Authority approved the project's budget, clearing a critical financial hurdle, and the Shaker Lane School Building Committee gathered Tuesday evening to advance the planning steps that follow. It is the kind of milestone that doesn't announce itself with fanfare, but quietly signals that something big is finally going to happen—and that Littleton's youngest learners will eventually have a school built for the century they're actually living in.

sections.body: With the MSBA's budget approval now in hand, the Shaker Lane Building Committee's July 22nd meeting marked the transition from advocacy to architecture—the hard, detail-oriented work of turning a community's hopes into a construction plan. The committee is operating against a backdrop of genuine urgency: a 64-year-old building was not designed for modern learning, accessibility, or energy standards, and Littleton families have waited a long time for this moment. The School Committee's Negotiating Subcommittee also convened Friday at the Reuben Hoar Library, a reminder that the human infrastructure of staffing and contracts runs alongside the physical work of building. Planning Board members met Thursday as well, continuing to shape the land-use context in which any new construction will eventually sit.

The school news this week wasn't only bricks and budgets. Littleton Middle School earned a National Blue Ribbon nomination and was ranked among the highest-performing schools in the state, while the high school received its own state recognition for educational excellence. Five Littleton students also earned state-level honors for achievement in world languages—a small but gratifying detail that puts faces on what district-wide recognition actually means. Taken together, these acknowledgments paint a picture of a school system that is doing something right even as it grapples with aging facilities.

The week also brought a painful counterpoint. A former Littleton school bus aide pleaded guilty to physically assaulting nonverbal autistic students during 2024. The admission in court closes a legal chapter, but the harm to those children and their families does not close so neatly. It is a reminder that excellence in outcomes and vigilance in safeguarding must go hand in hand.

On the conservation side of town life, this week brought something genuinely celebratory: the official opening of the Art Lazarus Trail at Long Lake Park Conservation Area. Named for a longtime conservation volunteer, the trail is the kind of civic gesture that costs little and lasts long—a path through the woods that carries a person's name and legacy into the future. The Littleton Conservation Trust invited the public to a ribbon-cutting ceremony, and the ongoing Littleton Trails Hiking Challenge gives residents a ready reason to lace up and explore it. The Conservation Commission met Tuesday night, continuing its steady work overseeing the natural resources that make trails like this one possible.

With the September 1st state primary approaching, the Town Clerk's office is reminding residents that in-person early voting is available. Primaries in off-cycle summers have a way of sneaking up on people, and this one is less than six weeks out. The Clerk's office has details on times and locations—worth a look before the summer gets any busier.

pull_quote: A 64-year-old school, a state budget approval, and a town finally ready to build something new.
threads: Watch the Select Board's Monday, July 27th meeting at Town Hall—the first regular board session after the MSBA budget approval, which may prompt discussion of next steps for Shaker Lane.
The September 1st state primary early voting window is open now; check the Town Clerk's office for schedule and eligibility details before the deadline arrives.

headline: A New School, a New Sewer, and a Town Running Dry
dek: *Littleton enters August with generational infrastructure projects in motion — and a drought that's putting everyday life on pause.*
lede: It was a week that underscored just how much is being built, debated, and strained in Littleton all at once. The Massachusetts School Building Authority approved the budget for a replacement Shaker Lane Elementary School — a milestone for a building that has stood for 64 years and long outlived its useful life. At the same time, the town cut the ribbon on a brand-new common sewer system, the product of nearly two years of construction and a $45 million investment that officials say will reshape the town center's economic future. And threading through all of it: a Level 3 Critical Drought that has banned all nonessential outdoor water use, a vivid reminder that even a town investing in its future has to reckon with the limits of its land.

sections.body:
The Shaker Lane Elementary project cleared a major hurdle this week when the Massachusetts School Building Authority signed off on the project budget, giving the town the state partnership it needs to move forward on replacing a 64-year-old building. The Shaker Lane School Building Committee met on July 22nd, and the School Committee's negotiating subcommittee convened days later — signs that the institutional machinery is now in motion. The project will require sustained community engagement in the months ahead, and a Conservation Commission public hearing on the Shaker Lane property is already on the calendar for August 18th.

The school news doesn't stop there. Littleton Middle School has been nominated for a National Blue Ribbon award, and the high school separately received a state-level commendation — a moment worth savoring as the district simultaneously grapples with the long work of rebuilding its elementary facilities.

After nearly two years of digging, the town's new Common Sewer System is fully operational. The $45 million project replaces septic systems in the town center — a change that removes a longstanding constraint on development and sets the stage for economic growth along Littleton's main corridors. The ribbon cutting marks an endpoint for construction disruption and, town officials hope, a starting line for what comes next. The Select Board and Finance Committee are meeting jointly on Monday, August 3rd, which may offer an early glimpse at how leadership is thinking about the fiscal landscape those investments have created.

Littleton's relationship with water is complicated right now. On one front, the Littleton Water Department has filed a federal lawsuit seeking to recover the $20.25 million it spent building a treatment plant to remove PFAS contamination from the Spectacle Pond drinking water supply — a fight to hold polluters accountable for costs that fell on local ratepayers. On another front, the town is deep in a Level 3 Critical Drought, with all nonessential outdoor water use prohibited. Lawn irrigation, car washing, and surface cleaning are all off the table for now. Residents with real estate tax bills due August 3rd have that deadline on their minds too, making for a week where the water department's challenges felt close to home in more ways than one.

Away from the meeting rooms, Littleton marked a quieter but meaningful moment: the formal dedication of the Art Lazarus Trail at Long Lake Park Conservation Area, honoring a volunteer who gave 33 years of service to local conservation. The Littleton Conservation Trust's ceremony put a name and a story to the miles of protected land that residents hike and paddle past without always knowing their history. It also sets a fitting backdrop for an upcoming free talk at Reuben Hoar Library on yard pesticides and the steep decline in monarch butterfly populations — a reminder that conservation isn't only about land acquisition, but about the choices made on every lawn in town.

The coming days are dense with civic activity. The Select Board and Finance Committee hold their joint session Monday evening; the Conservation Commission, Board of Assessors, and Historical Commission all meet Tuesday; and the Planning Board convenes Thursday. For residents tracking any of these threads — the school project, sewer financing, land use near conservation areas — the next two weeks offer ample opportunity to watch, and to weigh in.

pull_quote: A 64-year-old school, a brand-new sewer, a federal PFAS lawsuit, and a drought: Littleton is building its future while managing the costs of its past.
threads: Watch the August 3rd Select Board–Finance Committee joint meeting for signals on how the town plans to manage the fiscal aftermath of the $45 million sewer project.

With a Level 3 Critical Drought in effect, track whether conditions ease — or tighten further — as the region moves through August.

headline: Schools, Trails, and Cameras: Littleton's Busy August
dek: *A week when the town's future classrooms, conservation legacy, and public-safety tech all demanded attention at once.*
lede: Littleton's summer may feel quiet on the surface, but beneath it the machinery of town government is running hard. The biggest story is the one with the longest arc: the plan to replace the 64-year-old Shaker Lane Elementary School building is moving steadily through its paces, with the Massachusetts School Building Authority having approved the project budget and a Planning Board public hearing on the site's stormwater and site plan already scheduled for September 3rd. sections.body:
Replacing a six-decade-old elementary school is not a small undertaking, and this week's activity shows just how many threads must be woven together before a shovel breaks ground. The MSBA's budget approval is a critical milestone — it locks in a financial framework for a project that will shape the town for generations. Now the work shifts to the regulatory and design side: the Planning Board will take up the stormwater management permit and site plan at a public hearing on September 3rd, giving residents their first formal opportunity to weigh in on how the new building will sit on the land.

All of this unfolds against a backdrop of genuine pride in what Littleton's schools are already doing. A National Blue Ribbon nomination for the middle school and a state honor for the high school are reminders that the push for a new building is about sustaining a strong system, not rescuing a struggling one.

Conservation made its presence felt on multiple fronts. The headline moment was a celebratory one: the Littleton Conservation Trust officially opened the Art Lazarus Trail at Long Lake Park Conservation Area, named for a volunteer who contributed 33 years to the town's conservation work, from 1984 to 2017. It is the kind of community milestone that tends to get lost in the shuffle of permits and agendas, but it deserves to be marked — a trail named for a neighbor who showed up, year after year, because the land mattered to him.

Less celebratory, but equally important, is a free public talk coming to Reuben Hoar Library on the environmental and health risks of common yard pesticides, framed around their role in dramatic insect population declines. The Conservation Commission also met on August 4th and has a joint meeting with the Select Board on August 10th — and a public hearing focused on 35 Shaker Lane scheduled for August 18th, a reminder that the commission's work is never just philosophical. The Littleton Police Department released a statement this week updating residents on the town's Flock automated license plate camera system. The police chief's decision to put a statement out proactively suggests the department is aware of that tension. Residents who want to understand how the system is being used should look for that update on the town's public safety pages.

The week was also a busy one for routine but essential civic business. The Select Board and Finance Committee held a joint session on August 3rd, a pairing that almost always signals budget or capital planning discussions. The Planning Board met on August 6th. Looking ahead, the Park and Recreation Commission meets August 11th, the Board of Health on August 12th, and the Zoning Board of Appeals on August 20th — a full slate as summer winds down and fall planning picks up.

headline: A Town Building Its Future, One Project at a Time
dek: *From a long-awaited school replacement to a landmark sewer ribbon-cutting, Littleton is deep in the work of renewal this August.*
lede: The biggest story in Littleton right now isn't any single meeting or vote — it's the unmistakable sense that the town is in the middle of building something. The Massachusetts School Building Authority has approved the budget for a new Shaker Lane Elementary School, clearing a critical hurdle for replacing a 64-year-old building that has served the community well past its intended life. Across town, the $45 million Common Sewer System — years in the making — has been declared fully operational, already drawing economic interest to the downtown. And beneath all of it runs a harder story: Littleton's Water Department has filed a federal lawsuit seeking to recover the $20.25 million it spent cleaning PFAS contamination from a drinking water well, a reminder that not every cost a town bears should fall on its residents alone.

sections.body: With the MSBA's budget approval in hand, the Shaker Lane School project has momentum that felt uncertain not long ago. The Building Committee met in late July, and come September 3rd, the Planning Board will hold a public hearing on the stormwater management permit and site plan — the kind of technical but consequential step that turns an approved budget into an actual building. The Conservation Commission has also scheduled a public hearing on 35 Shaker Lane for August 18th, and the Select Board joined the Conservation Commission for a joint session on August 10th, signaling that multiple town bodies are coordinating carefully around the site. Parents and neighbors will want to watch these hearings closely: the decisions made now will shape what the school looks like for the next 60 years.

The school construction news lands in a week of broader good feeling about Littleton's public schools. Littleton Middle School has been nominated for a National Blue Ribbon award — one of the most prestigious recognitions in American K-12 education — and has separately been ranked among the top-performing schools in Massachusetts. Littleton High School received its own state-level honor. Water is the thread connecting several of this week's most significant stories. The sewer system ribbon-cutting marks the completion of a decade-defining infrastructure project, and town officials say it is already beginning to shape development patterns downtown — precisely the economic catalyst its advocates promised. At the same time, the Littleton Electric Light and Water Department has filed a federal lawsuit to recover the $20.25 million it spent building a PFAS treatment plant, a cost that should never have been the town's to bear. And on top of all that, a Level 3 Critical Drought has triggered a ban on all nonessential outdoor water use — no lawn irrigation, no car washing, no surface cleaning. The irony of celebrating a new sewer system while asking residents to conserve every drop is not lost on anyone paying attention.

Not all of this week's news was about budgets and bureaucracy. The Littleton Conservation Trust formally opened the Art Lazarus Trail at Long Lake Park Conservation Area, honoring a volunteer who gave 33 years of his life to conservation work in town. It's the kind of moment that doesn't make headlines outside Littleton but means everything inside it — a trail named for a neighbor, in a park that neighbors stewarded together. The Conservation Commission has been active on multiple fronts, with recent meetings and fresh minutes posted, and its joint session with the Select Board this week reflects how central environmental questions have become to nearly every major decision the town faces.

One quieter piece of good news: Littleton Electric Light and Water has been awarded a $285,522 state grant to replace six outdated electrical reclosers — the equipment that helps isolate faults on power lines and limit the scope of outages. It's unglamorous infrastructure, the kind that only gets noticed when it fails. But for Littleton and neighboring Boxborough, newer reclosers mean shorter outages and a more resilient grid, and securing state money to pay for it is exactly the kind of fiscal care that keeps municipal electric rates manageable.
